newsitem.title: CANADA: Direct Choice wins Canada TV satellite bid.
newsitem.headline: Direct Choice wins Canada TV satellite bid.

text.p: Canada's broadcast regulatory agency on Tuesday granted a third license for a direct-to-home satellite system, this time to a unit of Direct Choice T.V. Inc.

The license from the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) went to Direct Choice's Star Choice Television Network Inc to operate a national digital DTH satellite distribution system.
Direct Choice said in a statement two weeks ago that it intended to launch a DTH satellite service within months of receiving a CRTC license.

"Given the technical difficulties currently affecting Telesat Canada's Anik E1 satellite, Star Choice has worked out several scenarios to ensure an early delivery of Canadian programming services," the CRTC said in its announcement.
Telesat Canada is controlled by BCE Inc.
"Star Choice confirmed that all of its options would be in accordance with the Canadian government's satellite policy," the CRTC said.

The CRTC explained that government policy requires Canadian distributors -- except in the case of temporary technical problems -- to carry all Canadian programming services, while allowing them to use U.S. satellites to carry authorized American signals.

Star Choice's preferred interim satellite delivery option would be to sublease satellite capacity on Anik E2 from an existing customer, which would allow it to be in operation by the end of 1996, the CRTC said.
Non-Canadian programming would be supplied by U.S. satellites.
The other two DTH licenses were granted to ExpressVu and to Power DirecTv, but neither are up and running.
Power DirecTv, controlled by Power Corp of Canada, has decided against launching the service at least for now.

Expressvu Inc, owned by BCE Inc, Tee-Comm Electronics Inc, Canadian Satellite Communications Inc and WIC Western International Communications Ltd, has declined to say when it will begin its service because of regulatory and technical problems, one of which was the failure of the Anik E1 satellite.
Tee-Comm announced on August 15 that it had filed its own application with the CRTC to operate a DTH service.
